seo.title: Google's .eat and .here Domains: Worth Buying?
seo.meta_description: Google launched .eat, .fly and .here domains. Do eat and here domains help SEO? What Anaheim and Orange County businesses should know first.

h1: Google's New .eat and .here Domains: Should Orange County Businesses Buy One?
answer: Google's new eat and here domains, plus .fly, launched on November 10, 2026 through an Early Access Program and become publicly available on November 17. Google says new domain endings give no ranking advantage, so for Anaheim and Orange County businesses they are a branding choice, not an SEO shortcut.
key_takeaways: Google Registry launched .eat, .fly and .here on November 10, 2026.
Early Access prices fall daily until public availability on November 17.
Google says keywords in a domain ending give no search advantage.
Moving your main site is a site move with real risk.
A short memorable domain can still help branding and offline marketing.

sections.heading: What Google launched
sections.body_html: On November 10, 2026, Google Registry launched three new top-level domains: .eat, .fly and .here. Google describes them as clear, memorable web addresses that describe what a business does before anyone clicks. They are available through an Early Access Program, with prices decreasing daily until they become publicly available at a base annual rate on November 17, 2026.

sections.heading: What each ending is for
sections.body_html:
DomainHow Google frames itExamples Google cites
.eatBusinesses behind every meal, from restaurants to food brandswingstop.eat, xook.eat
.flyBusinesses on the move, from travel to aviation and AI toolscaddy.fly, voltair.fly
.herePlaces where people get things done, such as homes, jobs and servicesrent.here and sell.here (Zillow)

sections.heading: Do new domains help SEO?
sections.body_html: No. Google's Search Central team has said its systems treat new generic top-level domains like other generic endings such as .com and .org, and that keywords in a top-level domain do not give any advantage or disadvantage in search. Even endings that look regional are treated as generic. A restaurant does not rank better because its address ends in .eat.

sections.heading: Where they can still help
sections.body_html: A short, memorable address can be easier to say on the radio, print on a menu or remember from a truck. For example, an Anaheim restaurant might use a .eat address on table cards and in ads while its main website stays where it is. That is a branding decision, and it can be worth it, but it is not a ranking strategy.

sections.heading: The risk of moving your main site
sections.body_html: Switching your main website to a new domain is a site move. Google's site move documentation says to map old URLs to new ones, redirect them, monitor both, change only one thing at a time and expect temporary ranking fluctuations; for medium-sized sites it can take a few weeks or more to settle. Google's new-TLD guidance adds that domain changes can take time to be processed. For most local businesses with established rankings, that risk is not worth taking just for a new ending.

sections.heading: A safer approach
sections.body_html:
1. Keep your main website on its current domain.
  2. If you like a new ending, register it for campaigns or as a short link.
  3. Redirect it to the right page on your main site with a permanent redirect.
  4. Keep your Google Business Profile pointing at your main site.
  5. Track visits from the new address separately.

sections.heading: Defensive registration
sections.body_html: Some businesses register a new ending simply so nobody else uses their name on it. If your brand name is distinctive, check whether yourname.eat or yourname.here is available, especially if customers might reasonably expect it to be you.

sections.heading: What matters more for local search
sections.body_html: For Anaheim and Orange County businesses, the things that move local rankings are unchanged: a complete Business Profile, accurate listings, clear service pages and genuine reviews. Google's own local ranking help says results are mainly based on relevance, distance and popularity, and that there is no way to pay for a better local ranking.

sections.heading: What about AI assistants?
sections.body_html: AI assistants describe businesses from the content and listings they find, not from the domain ending. A memorable domain will not make ChatGPT or Google's AI features recommend you; clear, consistent information will.

sections.heading: Who might move to a new domain
sections.body_html: A brand-new business with no search history, or a business that is rebranding anyway, has less to lose and might choose a new ending from the start. Even then, follow Google's site move guidance if any old site exists, and keep the name consistent everywhere.

sections.heading: Questions to ask before you buy
sections.body_html:
• Will customers remember it more easily than our current address?
  • Where will we actually use it: print, ads, signage?
  • Will it redirect to a specific page?
  • Who will renew it each year?
  • Are we tempted to move our main site, and do we understand the risk?

sections.heading: How redirects should work
sections.body_html: If you use a new ending as a campaign address, point it at a specific page with a permanent redirect, for example yourname.eat sending visitors straight to your menu page. Do not build a second copy of your website on the new domain; duplicate sites split attention and confuse customers and search engines.

sections.heading: What it costs to hold a domain
sections.body_html: Google says the new endings will have a base annual rate once public, and Early Access prices fall each day until November 17. Factor renewal into the decision: a domain you stop renewing can be registered by someone else, so only buy names you are willing to keep.

sections.heading: Check availability safely
sections.body_html: Search for your name through a well-known registrar rather than unfamiliar sites, and be wary of unsolicited emails offering to secure a new domain for you. Google's announcement points businesses to their preferred registrar.

sections.heading: The short version
sections.body_html: The new .eat, .fly and .here domains are a branding option, not an SEO advantage. For most Anaheim and Orange County businesses, the smart move is to keep the main site where it is and, if useful, use a new ending as a redirecting campaign address.

faqs.a: On November 10, 2026, through an Early Access Program, with public availability on November 17, 2026.

faqs.q: Do new domain endings help Google rankings?
faqs.a: No. Google says keywords in a top-level domain give no advantage or disadvantage in search.

faqs.q: Should my restaurant switch to a .eat domain?
faqs.a: Usually not for SEO. A .eat address can work as a memorable campaign link that redirects to your main site.

faqs.q: Is moving my site to a new domain risky?
faqs.a: Yes. Google treats it as a site move, and rankings can fluctuate for weeks while it is processed.

faqs.q: What is the Early Access Program?
faqs.a: A period before public launch when available domains can be registered for a fee that decreases daily.

faqs.q: Do AI assistants care about domain endings?
faqs.a: They describe businesses from content and listings, not the domain ending.
Google frames it for places where people get things done, such as homes, jobs and services.

faqs.q: Should I register my brand name defensively?
faqs.a: If your name is distinctive and customers might expect it, it can be sensible.

faqs.q: Can I use a .here domain for my Google Business Profile?
faqs.a: Point your profile at your main website; if you use a new ending, redirect it to that site.
